profiles.meeting_scenario: An invited design review meeting for a journal article provisionally titled "The Capability Approach: a Theoretical Survey," being prepared for an interdisciplinary social policy journal's annual theory review issue. The paper is meant to introduce the capability approach across philosophy, economics, development studies, and public policy while remaining readable for non-specialists. The agenda is to review the current article blueprint—title, section structure, use of examples, framing devices, and submission-readiness—and decide whether the design is suitable for the journal's review issue or needs revision before the full draft is sent out. The expected outcome is a shared decision on whether the current structure can move forward as the submission version, plus a short list of revisions to make first.

members.name: Dr. Leila Haddad
members.expertise: Political philosophy, welfare theory, and comparative social justice
members.background: Leila is an associate professor who has published on Sen, Nussbaum, and evaluative frameworks in ethics and development studies; she is experienced in writing theoretical syntheses for academic audiences but less experienced with broad-audience journal formats.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve conceptual precision and avoid the paper turning into a simplified teaching primer; she also needs to keep the draft within a manageable scope because she is balancing this article with a grant deadline.
hidden_assumptions: "Accessible" in this context means understandable to scholars outside capability-approach scholarship, not to first-time readers with no background in normative theory.
A "theoretical survey" should stay mostly at the level of concepts, distinctions, and debates, with only one compact illustrative policy example near the end.
The journal's stated 8,000-word limit works like most philosophy-oriented review venues she knows: excluding references, notes, and display elements such as breakout boxes.

A manuscript is "ready for review" once the conceptual architecture and core prose are in place; copy-level apparatus like glossary language, permissions, and final cross-disciplinary signposting can be added after peer review.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.role: Commissioning Editor for the Theory Review Issue
members.expertise: Interdisciplinary academic editing, journal positioning, and reader-oriented article design
members.background: Evan manages invited reviews for a social policy journal read by academics, advanced practitioners, and doctoral students across several fields; he routinely helps authors reshape specialist material into issue-wide accessible formats.
members.private_state: He wants this piece to function as the entry-point article of the issue and be usable by readers from economics, public health, and policy analysis without relying on prior philosophy training; he is also trying to avoid production problems after a recent style-policy update.
hidden_assumptions: "Accessible" means a reader from outside normative theory should be able to follow the paper continuously without looking up foundational terms.
A "theoretical survey" for this issue should integrate concrete examples throughout so readers can see how the concepts travel into policy and social evaluation contexts.
The current review-issue template's 8,000-word cap is all-inclusive, including references, abstract, author note, and any callout boxes, because production now counts total typeset space.

A manuscript is "ready for external review" only if the issue-specific framing is already built in: glossary-like first mentions, stable section headings, finalized examples, and no later-added structural devices that could change review judgments.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an accessible article
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the paper should be "accessible" and "usable outside the specialty."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leila means the paper should avoid unnecessary jargon and explain core distinctions well enough for scholars in adjacent disciplines who already read theory-heavy work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan means the paper should be readable as a true entry point for readers with little or no background in political philosophy, including advanced practitioners and doctoral students outside the theory literature.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both positively value accessibility, and neither interpretation sounds unreasonable in an interdisciplinary journal setting; because they share the same approving language, the difference in implied reader baseline never gets explicitly unpacked.

misalignment_points.topic: Where examples belong in a theoretical survey
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the paper will include "a policy example" and remain a "theoretical survey."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leila assumes one brief, contained example—likely around disability or education—will appear in the conclusion or a short inset, while the rest of the paper stays concept-first.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan assumes each major section will carry at least a small concrete application so the survey continuously translates concepts into policy-relevant interpretation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They appear aligned because both endorse having examples and preserving the paper's theoretical identity; the disagreement concerns the boundary of where examples belong, which feels too implementation-level to spell out in an otherwise smooth review meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer casually to "staying within the 8,000 words" and using the "standard review format."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leila presupposes the cap applies to main text only, with references, notes, and any breakout box material treated separately as in many theory reviews.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan presupposes the cap is all-inclusive under the journal's newer production rules, including references and display elements because all consume layout space.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Word limits are usually treated as settled administrative background rather than a substantive design issue, so each assumes the shared phrase already points to one obvious institutional standard.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss getting the piece "ready for external review" next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leila believes review readiness means the argument structure, section sequence, and main prose are stable enough for reviewers to assess the intellectual contribution, while polish and reader aids can follow later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Evan believes review readiness requires the article already to contain the audience-facing architecture reviewers will judge—glossed terminology, fixed examples, issue-style headings, and finalized framing choices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In many academic workflows, 'ready for review' is a familiar milestone that participants rarely define; each believes they are invoking the normal standard for scholarly submission, so the underlying criteria remain implicit.

turns.inner_thought: This piece will open the issue, so it has to work as a genuine entry point for readers in economics, public health, and policy who may have no philosophy training at all. I need to confirm not just intellectual quality but that the article is accessible in that broad sense, and I need the next version to be ready for external review in the full issue format, not merely intellectually drafted.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Leila. Since this is likely to sit near the front of the theory review issue, I mainly want to check that the current blueprint feels accessible and usable outside the specialty, and that we're on track to have it ready for external review soon.

turns.inner_thought: I should emphasize coherence and scope control. The paper needs to introduce the central architecture without turning into a textbook chapter. My plan is a concept-led survey: origins, capabilities versus functionings, means versus ends, then major contributors and disputes, with one compact application at the end—probably disability or education—just enough to anchor the discussion without letting examples take over.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. The structure I have is fairly clean: a short opening on the origins of the capability approach, then sections on capabilities and functionings, means and ends, and the main lines of development across key contributors. I end with a policy example so it remains a theoretical survey but still shows where the framework lands.

turns.inner_thought: The outline is promising, but every section has to carry readers who don't already know normative theory. I want the piece to read smoothly for policy and development people from start to finish, not only become concrete at the end.
turns.utterance: That sounds strong to me. My only broad steer is that each section should stay accessible for readers coming in from policy and development, not just theory, so the piece keeps its footing across the whole issue.

turns.inner_thought: That's reasonable. I can certainly avoid unnecessary specialist shorthand and define the core distinctions carefully. But I don't want to flatten the argument by explaining every elementary term in moral and political theory as if readers have never encountered normative vocabulary.
turns.utterance: I agree. I've already pared back a lot of specialist phrasing, and I'll make sure the main distinctions are defined clearly on first use so it's accessible without becoming overburdened.

turns.inner_thought: If we thread examples through the major sections, readers will understand why the distinctions matter. I don't want a single application tagged on after pages of abstraction. But I can signal this gently by talking about a policy example helping the argument all the way through.
turns.utterance: Good. I also think concrete material will help it travel. If there's a policy example in the piece, that usually makes the argument easier to follow all the way through while still keeping it as a theoretical survey.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, one concise example near the conclusion will satisfy that without forcing every section into case-based exposition. Disability would work well because it is already central in the literature; education could also be compact. The key thing is not to let the paper sprawl.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can add a concise disability or education policy example toward the end, so readers have an application in view while the paper remains a theoretical survey.

turns.inner_thought: I also need to protect production. Under the updated template, the 8,000-word cap is total typeset space, so any framing aids, boxes, abstract, and references all matter. If she's at 7,400 before those, we're in trouble unless she trims. I'll phrase it as reassurance that the standard review format can accommodate the needed apparatus.
turns.utterance: Great. On the practical side, as long as we stay within the standard 8,000 words, I think the extra framing devices should fit comfortably in the review format.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine. The main prose is already around 7,400, which gives me enough room to finish the argument. References and any small text box shouldn't be part of that cap in the ordinary review setup, so I don't see a problem.
turns.utterance: That should be manageable. The main narrative is already about 7,400 words, so I should be able to stay within the 8,000 words under the standard review format, especially if any small add-ons are handled in the usual way.

turns.inner_thought: I need the next file to be the actual review version—stable section headings, audience-facing framing, examples placed where they'll remain, and first-mention explanations in place. Reviewers will judge the piece as it appears, and I don't want major architectural additions later.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Looking ahead to next week, do you think that version can be the one that's ready for external review, with the headings and the issue-facing framing in place?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, if by review-ready we mean the conceptual structure and prose are complete. I can have the argument fully written and organized by then. Smaller reader aids—glossary-style touches, any permissions questions, fine-grained signposting—are exactly the sort of things I'd normally refine after reports come back.
turns.utterance: Yes, next week should be realistic for getting it ready for external review. The argument map will be settled, the full prose will be there, and I can then make any smaller presentation refinements in the normal course.

turns.inner_thought: Good—then we're aligned, at least as I understand it: a broadly accessible entry-point survey, concrete grounding throughout, and a near-final package for reviewers next week. That would keep the issue schedule intact.
turns.utterance: Excellent. I'm glad we're aligned on an accessible theoretical survey with a policy example and a version that's close enough to final to go out on that timeline.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds fine. I'll keep the piece rigorous and restrained, deliver the substantive draft next week, and trust that any final framing apparatus can be layered in without changing the core article. As long as the standard review format behaves as expected, the scope remains manageable.
turns.utterance: Good. I'll work to that plan and send the revised version next week under the standard review format, keeping it conceptually rigorous while still broadly readable.
